pg011_p012: The concept of the book of Exodus
pg011_p013: The book of Exodus is one of the five books of the Pentateuch. It is the second book in the canonical arrangement of the books of the Bible. In it, we find the stories of the life of Hebrews in Egypt: prosperity and oppression, the birth, call, and mission of Moses. There is also a story of the Ten Plagues and the first Passover. In addition, the book continues recounting the departure of God’s children to the Promised Land, the parting of the Red Sea, the covenant at Sinai, the Ten Commandments and the story of the apostasy.
pg011_p020: The name and authorship of the book
pg011_p021: The name “Exodus” comes from the Greek word “ἔξοδος” (exodos), which translates to “going out” or “departure.” The book gets its name from the event of the Israelites’ departure from Egypt to the Promised Land (Exodus 12:29-15:21). The Hebrew name for the book is “Shemot” which means names, referring to the list of the names of the sons of Israel who went down into Egypt with Jacob. Traditionally, the book is ascribed to Moses as the author. The book consists of 40 chapters.
pg011_p028: Exodus is primarily written as a revelation of God’s love and compassion. The book recounts Israelites sufferings and liberation from slavery in Egypt, their covenant with God on Mount Sinai, the preparation to enter the Promised Land as well as

pg016_p036: The birth, call, and mission of Moses
pg016_p037: Moses’ father was Amram, the grandson of Levi, while his mother was Jochebed

pg017_p008: The Egyptian prophets predicted the birth of a leader who would liberate the Israelites from slavery. This prediction resulted to the Pharaoh’s instruction toward the killing of all baby boys from Hebrew families at birth. Unfortunately, the inflicted edict against the innocent baby boys failed due to divine intervention. During the course of Pharaoh’s inhumane instruction, Amram’s wife gave birth to her third child, a baby boy, Moses. His parents tried all means to save the child from being killed by
pg017_p014: Pharaoh. After all efforts, Amram and Jochebed, the baby’s parents, realized that they could no longer hide the baby. Therefore, Jochebed made a small basket from bulrushes and bitumen. The basket was a waterproof vessel in which she put the baby and set him down among the Papyrus reeds on the bank of the Nile River.
pg017_p018: While Jochebed tearfully returned home, her daughter Miriam remained nearby to watch over the baby.
pg017_p020: The day was hot and king Pharaoh’s daughter (Bithya) came down to the river accompanied by her maids to take birth in the cool waters of the Nile. Suddenly, she heard the wailing of a small child. At that moment, she found the basket that had an infant baby boy in it. She realized that the baby was one of the babies born of Hebrews. Intrigued by the beauty of the child, Pharaoh’s daughter made arrangements to bring it up in a royal court. While this was happening, there aside was a girl. The girl asked Pharaoh’s daughter if she could get a Hebrew nurse for the child. The girl also run to ask Jochebed to present herself to Pharaoh’s daughter as a maid to nurse the found child. Thus, the child continued being nursed by its mother, and when he grew up, he was brought into Pharaoh’s palace, where the Pharaoh’s daughter brought him up as her own son. Finally, she named him Moses means drawn out of the water (Exodus 2:5-10).

pg018_p005: Although Moses was brought up in the royal house and regarded as the son of
pg018_p006: Pharaoh’s daughter, he was aware of his origin. When he grew up, he killed an
pg018_p007: Egyptian overseer who was beating a Hebrew slave. In another occasion, he saw two Hebrews fighting, when he rebuked them, one of them said “…do you mean to kill me as you killed that Egyptian?’ (Exodus 2:14).
pg018_p010: When Pharaoh heard of this murder story, he plotted to kill Moses. To rescue his life, Moses fled to Midian. While in Midian, his bravery won him a wife, Zipporah, a daughter of the priest of Midian. Moses got a wife after defending the seven daughters of Reu’el (Jethro) the priest of Midian from the shepherds who drove them away from the well. Zipporah bore Moses two sons. The first one was named
pg018_p015: Gershom (meaning ‘I am a sojourner in a foreign land’, Exodus 2:11-22), the second son was Eliezer (meaning ‘the God of my father was my help’ Exodus 18:4).
pg018_p018: God prepared Moses for a special redemptive mission. He was adopted and raised in the house of the daughter of Pharaoh. He had the best education of the known ancient Egyptian world. Egypt was, at that time, one of the most productive and progressive countries of the known world, with the best educational achievements attained among the lands of the ancient world. Their economic and social life, too, was highly advanced. This was the environment in which Moses was raised up from his youth. A transition from the royal court of Pharaoh to the backside of the desert would have been a drastic change for anyone, but God had a purpose in Moses’ development. God was going to make Moses His instrument in the redemptive plan, though after some years of divine formation.
pg018_p028: For forty years, Moses was in the courts of Pharaoh learning Egyptian wisdom, power structures and instruments of governance. Nevertheless, God had a different alternative through which His people were to be delivered from their slavery in
pg018_p031: Egypt. Although Moses spent another forty years in Midian, tending his father-in-law’s flock, he remained a common shepherd until when God finally changed the cause of his life and leadership over his fellow countrymen and women. In other words, Moses was exposed to a new divine call, reality, and mission that required his personal submission to God rather than depending on his previous educational prejudices or social status.

pg019_p005: Moses was called at the age of 80 as recorded in Exodus 7:7. He experienced his call through the unconsumed burning bush at Horeb, the mountain of God (Exodus 3:1-6). Moses’ encounter with the unconsumed burning bush is a typical manifestation of the fact that divine leadership is about serving the God of the universe. It was through this encounter that Moses became fully aware that God was present with him and that he was called to serve God’s people and purposes. Surprised by the unconsumed burning bush, Moses turned aside to see what that strange thing was.
pg019_p012: As the Bible says, “And when the Lord saw that he turned aside to see, God called to him out of the burring bush ‘Moses, Moses …put off your shoes from your feet for the place you are standing is holy ground” (Exodus 3:1-6).

pg021_p016: The first sign was of the rod turning into a serpent. The Lord asked Moses to look at what he was holding. Moses saw that it was his familiar rod with which he had daily tended the sheep. God told Moses to cast the rod down and to step back. Moses obeyed the Lord, and the rod turned into a serpent. Moses was startled at the sight of the serpent, but the Lord told him to pick it up. Moses knew from his Egyptian background that the only way to pick up a serpent was by the head, so that it could not bite him. However, the Lord told Moses to pick it up by the tail. In the very act of picking up the serpent by the tail instead of the head, Moses was learning obedience to God’s commands in contrast to the ways of Egypt. Moses was learning that it was not going to be by Egyptian reasoning or logic that he would deliver Israel, but by
pg021_p026: God’s Word and Spirit. The fear and unbelief that Moses showed was answered by
pg021_p027: God through his miraculous experience with the rod. The other two signs of leprosy and water turning into blood also showed Moses that the most common things in the hands of man become opportunities for the Lord to show forth His power when they are submitted to His command. In a similar way, God teaches every one of His leaders that His Spirit is the key to ministry’s success.
pg021_p033: Moses’ fourth response to the call of the Lord was that he was unable to speak
pg021_p034: (Exodus 4:10-17). “And Moses said to the Lord, “I am not eloquent…. I am slow of speech, and of a slow tongue.” This inability to speak is quite a contrast to Moses of forty years earlier who was a man “mighty in words.” Moses had lost all confidence in himself as a spokesman. In response to this, the Lord appointed Aaron the brother to Moses as a spokesperson.
pg022_p005: Moses’ fifth excuse to the calling of the Lord was an attitude of inferiority. Moses believed that the Lord had made a mistake in His choice, “And he said, “O Lord send, I pray, some another person” (Exodus 4:13). Moses was not the same proud prince of the Egyptian kingdom he had once been. He was now acting like a humble shepherd from the backside of the desert who had been stripped of all his pride and self-confidence. In the end, God gave Moses his brother Aaron to be his mouthpiece, not out of His wisdom, but simply to satisfy Moses’ endless requests. Moreover,
pg022_p012: Aaron would always be a reminder to his brother that he must always depend upon
pg022_p013: God’s help and strength in his ministry.
pg022_p015: Moses’ last response to God’s calling was his accusation against the Lord because of no apparent fruitfulness in what the Lord had told him to do. In Exodus 5:21-22,
pg022_p017: Moses went to Egypt and spoke the words that the Lord had told him to speak. What
pg022_p018: Moses had expected to happen did not happen, and he was profoundly disappointed.
pg022_p019: Indeed, things became worse. Pharaoh did not hearken to the words of the Lord through Moses and Aaron. Pharaoh had the taskmasters beat the children of Israel because of what Moses had said. Moses was displeased because of this apparent unfruitfulness in his ministry. But at this point, the Lord was testing Moses to see the kind of reaction he would demonstrate. Moses expected results sooner than the
pg022_p024: Lord wanted to give them. Moses was learning patience.
pg022_p026: The primary mission of Moses was liberation of the sons of Israel from slavery in Egypt and lead them to the Promised Land. However, he was to face Pharaoh the king of Egypt with two-fold mission: First, to demand for the liberation of the enslaved Hebrews, in this regard, to tell Pharaoh to let the people go. Second, through him God wanted to teach Pharaoh that the gods they worshiped are not gods at all. The Lord out of the burning bush appointed Moses to fulfil these tasks.
pg022_p032: After Pharaoh was humbled with the ten plagues, he let the people go, here the task of Moses was to lead the people on the way to the Promised Land and to become a mediator between God and His people.
pg022_p035: Briefly, we see that throughout the journey of our discussion from the prosperity of the sons of Israel to the call of Moses, it is a reflection on God’s love and compassion, not only for the people of Israel but also for His creation at large. It is an invitation to see that God is always at work for the sustainability and salvation of his people.

pg023_p007: The Ten Plagues: Revelation of God’s power
pg023_p008: After Pharaoh refused to let the people of Israel go and offer sacrifice to the Lord, the land of Egypt was inflicted with Ten Plagues. The ten plagues are a series of catastrophic events through which the Lord humbled the Egyptians. On one side
pg023_p011: God revealed Himself as the only and mighty God, and on the other side proved to the Egyptians that the gods and goddess they believed were not gods. Again, with these catastrophic events the Lord wanted to set free His people from slavery in
pg023_p014: Egypt. It was a revelation of God’s love and compassion to His people Israel.
pg023_p015: Number ten is a significant number in biblical numerology. It represents a fullness of quantity. The ten Egyptian Plagues means Egypt was completely plagued. Just as the “Ten Commandments” become symbolic of the fullness of the moral law of
pg023_p018: God, the ten ancient plagues of Egypt represent the fullness of God’s expression of justice and judgments upon those who refuse to repent. Through the plagues,
pg023_p020: Pharaoh was given an opportunity to let the Israelites go. Moses and Aaron were sent as messengers to Pharaoh, to instruct him to let the Israelites go so that they may serve the Lord freely. Each plague corresponds to each Egyptian gods and goddess.

pg024_p007: The first plague: Water Turned into Blood
pg024_p008: This plague was to prove that the Egyptian god “Hopi”, god (spirit) of the Nile,
pg024_p009: “Khnum”, the guardian of the Nile, and “Osiris” the giver of life whose bloodstream was Nile were not gods. As Aaron, the spokesman for Moses, stretched the “rod” of the Lord over the water of Egypt, Nile River, other rivers and all other sources of water in Egypt turned into blood. The water became unsuitable for drinking, all the fish died, and the rivers stank. The magicians of Pharaoh also turned water into blood, leaving Pharaoh unimpressed with this great wonder from God. For seven days the water throughout all the land of Egypt remained in this state, unsuitable for drinking, the perfect length of time to demonstrate that the Lord was superior to all the gods of Egypt (Exodus 7:14-25).
pg024_p018: The second plague: Frogs coming from the Nile River
pg024_p019: This plague intended to prove that the Egyptian goddess “Heqt” is not god. This
pg024_p020: Egyptian goddess, a form of a frog was regarded as the god of resurrection who assisted women in child birth. The frogs came up from the rivers and were in their houses, in their food, in their clothing, in every place possible. From the greatest to the least, no one in Egypt escaped the plague of frogs. Pharaoh’s magicians were able to bring more frogs in their attempt to imitate the power of God, but only Moses was able to make the frogs go away (Exodus 8:1-15).
pg024_p027: This plague intended to prove that the Egyptian god “Geb”, god of the earth is not god. It was believed that the Egyptian god “Geb” was over the dust of the earth. At the command of the Lord to Moses, Aaron was told to stretch forth his rod and smite the dust of the earth. When he did the dust became gnats throughout the land, on both people and beasts. The very dust that was referred to in the creation process of man is now used to plague men, as a reminder of his mortality and sin which both lead to death. Finally, the magicians of Pharaoh are humiliated, being unable to compete with this power. They said: “This is the finger of God” This was the last plague that required Aaron’s involvement, as the next set of three plagues are issued by the word of Moses himself (Exodus 8:16-19).

pg025_p004: The fourth plague: Swam of flies
pg025_p005: This plague intended to prove that “Khepri” the Egyptian god who had a head of a fly is not god. For the Egyptians this was a god of creation, movement of the sun, and rebirth (Exodus 8:20-32). After seeing the intensity of the plague, Pharaoh bargained that they can go to sacrifice their God but in the land of Egypt something which was not accepted by Moses.

pg025_p013: The fifth plague: Death of livestock
pg025_p014: Moses once again demanded Pharaoh, “Let my people go, that they may serve me”, revealing also the next Egyptian plague to occur on the condition of continued disobedience to the request. This plague was against “Hathor” - Egyptian goddess of love and protection who had a form of a cow. The plague also was against “Apis”
pg025_p018: – the bull god regarded as the creator god and symbol of fertility. This plague was given with an advanced warning, allowing a period of repentance to occur, which goes unheeded. “Tomorrow” the hand of the Lord would be felt upon all the cattle and livestock, of only the Egyptians.” This means that disease and pestilence would fall upon their cattle and cause them to die. This plague affected the Egyptians by creating a huge economic disaster, in areas of food, transportation, military supplies, farming, and economic goods that were produced by these livestock. Still Pharaoh’s heart remained hard and he would not listen to the Lord but remained attached to the
pg025_p028: Ashes turned to boils and sores. This plague was against Egyptian goddess of medicine and peace “Imhotep.” Announcement of the sixth Egyptian plague is given, for the first time, directly attacking the Egyptian people themselves. Being instructed by the Lord, Moses took ashes from the kiln-furnace of affliction (Furnace of affliction was a centre of heating, used to smelt ore, melt metal for castings, heating metal for forging, fire pottery or bricks and used to make lime. It was further used for smelting ore or for firing bricks), and threw them into the air. As the dust from the ashes blew all over Egypt, it settled on man and beast alike in the form of boils and sores. As was for the previous two plagues, the division is drawn between the
pg025_p037: Egyptians and the children of Israel, as God gives protection to His covenant people.
pg025_p038: The severity of the judgment of God has now become personal, as it is actually felt by the people themselves. Cleanliness being paramount in the Egyptian society, this

It is great to notice the contrast shown as Moses and Aaron are the only ones left standing in front of Pharaoh, with the “One True God” as their support (Exodus 9:8-12).

pg026_p012: Hail rained down in the form of fire. This was against “Nut”- Egyptian goddess of the sky. This plague was also against “Isis” the goddess of life and “Seth” the protector of crops. Again, warning is given before the enactment of the plague. Pharaoh was warned of the impending doom that will be faced if he does not listen to the Lord, and forget his own Egyptian gods and goddesses. Before the plague through Moses the Lord even warned Pharaoh to bring back all that is in the field, cattle and human beings alike. The plague came down in thunder, hail and fire (Exodus 9:13-35).
pg026_p020: Locusts sent from the sky. This was a plague against “Seth” – Egyptian god of storms and disorder, and was also regarded as protector of crops. And the plague was also against Isis the god of life who had a head of locust. The eighth plague issued by the Lord had greater impact than the previous plague. It was to be felt so that Pharaoh would tell even “his sons and son’s sons” the mighty things of the Lord, thus, teaching even future generations of the power of the “strong hand of God” over

pg027_p004: all the Egyptian gods and goddesses (Exodus 10:1-20). This was the second wave of destruction to follow the hail, and whatever crops were left intact after that display, were now completely consumed by the swarms of locusts that were unleashed from the sky. This wonder definitely affected their life source. By hitting them in their food supply, the Lord displayed the possibility of eminent death if a change of heart did not occur. Yet still, Pharaoh could not listen.
pg027_p010: The ninth plague: Three days of complete darkness
pg027_p011: This plague was against “Ra-Re, Aten, Atum and Horus” – all these regarded as sun gods. Darkness fell upon Egypt, unannounced, as a prelude to the future fate to be felt by the Egyptian empire when the message of the Lord was not heeded, and they still turned to their own Egyptian gods and goddesses. Three days of palpable darkness, that was so immense it could be physically felt, covered the land of Egypt.
pg027_p016: The sun, the most worshipped god in Egypt other than Pharaoh himself, gave no light. The Lord showed that he had control over the sun as a witness that the God of Israel had ultimate power over life and death. Darkness was a representation of death, judgement and hopelessness (Exodus 10:21-29).
pg027_p020: The Tenth plague: Death of the firstborn
pg027_p021: Pharaoh, the king of Egypt, was worshipped by the Egyptians because he was considered to be the greatest of all the Egyptian gods. It was believed that he was actually the son of “Ra-Re” himself manifested in the flesh. The plague was also against Osiris- giver of life.
pg027_p025: After the plague of darkness felt throughout the land was lifted, Pharaoh resumed his position of “bargaining with the Lord” and offered Moses another “deal”. Since all Egyptians’ animals had been consumed by the judgments of the Lord, Pharaoh now consented to the request made, to let the people go. But, they must leave their livestock behind. This was a totally unacceptable offer, as the animals were to be used as sacrifice to the Lord. Enraged, Pharaoh, pronounced the last deadly plague to be unleashed upon the land from his very own lips as he warns Moses, “Get away from me, take heed to yourself, see my face no more; for in that day, you see my face you shall die.” And Moses said, thus says the Lord, about midnight I will go out into the midst of Egypt and all the firstborn in the land of Egypt shall die, from the firstborn of Pharaoh that sits upon his throne, even to the firstborn of the maidservant that is behind the mill; and all the firstborn of beasts. And there shall be a great cry throughout all the land of Egypt, such as there was none like it, nor shall be like it anymore” (Exodus 11-12:32).

pg028_p006: The Passover feast was established as a memorial of liberation from slavery in
pg028_p007: Egypt. The Passover feast explains how God passed over the houses of the Israelites, sprinkled with blood as he struck the first born of Egyptians. Furthermore, at this point the passive obedience that the children of Israel have shown is now moved to a level of active obedience. They are given strict instructions to follow so that they do not also feel the judgment of this last plague sent by the Lord. These instructions are known as: The Feast of Passover, the Feast of Unleavened Bread, and the Law of the Firstborn. The Paschal lamb shall be slaughtered in the evening of the 14th day of the month (Nissan). Some of the blood to be put on the two doors’ posts and the lintel of the houses which they shall eat. The meat to be eaten at night should be roasted. The lamb was to be eaten with unleavened bread and bitter herbs. Nothing to be kept till the morning. They shall eat with loans gilded, sandals on the feet, staff on hand and shall be eaten in haste.

pg029_p009: Lessons from the event of plundering the Egyptians
pg029_p010: The act of plundering Egyptians has a lot to teach people. First, when the Israelites received these possessions was a fulfilment of God’s promise to Abraham to make him and his descendants prosperous. God is shown to be faithful to His promise.
pg029_p013: Second, the plundering of Egyptians is one of God’s mighty works of the exodus.
pg029_p014: Along with the plagues, it is a means by which God humbled the haughty Egyptians.
pg029_p015: The wonders of the exodus proclaim to the world that the God of Israel is the one true God, ruler of all nations.
pg029_p017: Third, this transfer of wealth is a judgment on Egyptians and example of God’s justice in action. By enslaving the Israelites, the pharaohs deprived them of the fruits of their labour. The pharaohs are also guilty of robbing God, the rightful master of
pg029_p020: Israel and the one entitled to Israel’s service. The gifts given to the Israelites at their departure compensated their labour and punished the crimes of Egypt.

pg030_p022: After Pharaoh let out of Egypt the sons of Israel, he changed his mind. So, he mounted his chariots and army to pursue the Israelites. When the Israelites saw the

pg031_p006: The people left the Sea of Reeds to the wilderness of Shur. They walked for three days and found water. The journey in the wilderness was the first test of God to His people. God put human beings in the position to show their loyalty (Exodus 15:22).
pg031_p010: When they arrived at Marah the Israelites found bitter water that they could not drink. Here the people murmured against Moses saying ‘what shall we drink?’
pg031_p012: When Moses cried to the Lord, He showed him a tree and he threw it into the water, and the water became suitable to drink. The murmuring of the people was a sign of distrust and unfaithfulness; they had no strong faith. Because of the challenges they experienced, they quickly forgot the mighty works God did in Egypt and at the Sea of Reeds (Exodus 15:23-26).
pg031_p017: From Marah the Israelite’s journey took them to Elim, where they found seven palm trees and twelve springs of water. Israel camped by twelve springs (Exodus. 15:27).
pg031_p020: In the wilderness of Sin, the people murmured again against Moses and Aaron for the lack of food, actually the murmuring was against God. In response to their murmuring the Lord sent manna and quail to feed them (Exodus 16:1-36).
pg032_p005: Manna is a fine flake like hoarfrost which God provided as food on the 40 years wandering in the desert. It is food from heaven that God fed the Israelites. It is a miraculous food that the Lord provided to feed His people on the way to the
pg032_p008: Promised Land. Here the people are tested on their willingness to comply with
pg032_p009: God’s instructions and obedience to God’s laws.
pg032_p011: There were regulations given by God as regards to manna. First of all, the people were to gather that everyone has enough to eat an omer for each person and nothing to be left until morning. Omer is a tenth measure of the ephah or a dry measure used to measure dry goods like grain. Manna was gathered every morning. Additionally, the Israelites were told that, a day before the Sabbath they were to gather twice than the other days. In all forty years of wandering in the desert no Manna fell on the Sabbath, however, some people went out to collect manna on the Sabbath, nonetheless, they found nothing.
pg032_p020: The food from heaven had peculiar characteristics. It fell in the morning only, then, it was so sweet like bread made of honey. Manna did not fall on the Sabbath.

The proclamation highlighted God’s compassion and his willingness to forgive, even when the Israelites have transgressed. pg034_p008: Appointment of Judges over the people
pg034_p009: On the way to the Promised Land, Moses met his father-in-Law. When Jethro saw everything that Moses had to do, he said, “You are not doing it the right way. You will wear yourself out and these people as well. This is too much for you to do alone.
pg034_p012: You should choose some capable men and appoint them as leaders of the people:
pg034_p013: They must be God-fearing men who can be trusted and who cannot be bribed. Let them serve as judges for the people on a permanent basis. pg034_p018: Moses took Jethro’s advice and chose capable men among all the Israelites. He appointed them as leaders of thousands, hundreds, fifties, and tens. They served as judges for the people on a permanent basis, bringing the difficult cases to Moses but deciding the smaller disputes themselves (Exodus 18:1-27).
pg034_p022: The above passage teaches that, in leadership there is a need to delegate power.

pg034_p025: The consequences of not appreciating God’s love and compassion
pg034_p026: Failing to appreciate God’s love and compassion, not only leads to idolatry, but degenerates living. It begins with thanklessness and indifferences and results in the lowering our standards. St. Paul in Romans 1:21 says that being unthankful to God is a corner stone of our sins. It is the way which leads to covetousness, worshiping creatures instead of God. The book of Exodus is clear on the consequences of not appreciating God’s love and compassion.

pg037_p026: Man has God as its origin or initiator. That is to say, God invites man to enter into a covenant and man responds to God’s invitation. pg049_p026: The Concept of Statistics and Census in the book of Numbers
pg049_p027: The book of Numbers does not give a scientific explanation of statistics and census; however, it provides crucial indicators pertaining to the practice of data collection and reporting in the ancient Israel. The book highlights the significance of organised

pg050_p004: and systematic record-keeping in the life of the community. The book consists of two major censuses, the first one was taken two years after the Israelites departed from Egypt (Numbers 1), the second one seems to had been conducted thirty-eight years later (Numbers 26:51-65). Strategically, the purpose of the two censuses was to form a community-driven military organization and to facilitate an equitable division of the Promised Land.
pg050_p010: The Censuses were equally used for the following strategic reasons: (1) They were essential for military preparation, and identifying all eligible men for military service. This ensured that the community is ready for any conflict that they might have faced during their journey. (2) Improving tribal structure by organizing the people according to their tribes and clans. Essentially, this demographic move helped to maintain the social and familial structure of the Israelite community. This structural organization was crucial for managing the logistics of their encampment and travel. (3) The census was also essential for meticulous record-keeping. The censuses in the book of Numbers shows the community’s documentation, and listing the demography of each tribe. Numbers 1:20-46, provides a detailed breakdown of the census’ results, and lists the number of men in each tribe. For example, Numbers
pg050_p021: 1:21 records that the number of men from the tribe of Reuben was 46,500. (4) Like the first account of the census, the second census also aimed at preparing the nation for equitable division of the Promised Land among the tribes of Israel. The land was divided according to the size of the population.
pg050_p025: What do we learn from the censuses conducted in the book of Numbers? A number of lessons can be drawn from a well conducted census such as the ones we are studying in the book of Numbers: (1) Accuracy- the detailed demographic work in this book highlights the importance of accuracy in data collection. Each tribe’s numbers were recorded precisely, ensuring that the community had a clear understanding of its composition. (2) Transparency- a comprehensive data collection process undertaken provides a population’s characteristics entail the fact that the entire process was transparent. As a result, everyone in the community had an opportunity to observe their demographics, housing and economic situation. (3) Comprehensiveness- the meticulous record-keeping reflects the comprehensiveness of the employed data collection process, and precisely capturing the entire community’s demographic details (4) The census data also played a crucial role in public resource allocation.

pg054_p004: Statistics, Census and Resource Management in Ancient Israel
pg054_p005: From their nature in the book of Numbers, statistics and census intended to identify how much human resources the community had and what consumptions needed for such community. In Numbers, the census was conducted not only for military purposes but also for the natural and residential resources management and distribution. Drawing upon this perspective, the census conducted in the book of Numbers aimed to lay down the ground for resources management among the people of Israel in the following ways: fair distribution of natural resources and logical investigation and planning.
pg054_p013: As the Israelites embarked toward the Promised Land, they were still facing a challenge relating to settlement. So, they needed a fair mechanism for distribution of the land in Canaan. The census conducted was strategically meant to establish the exact number of people in each of the twelve tribes of Israel. Thus, the census enabled distribution of the land and natural resources according to the family size and needs of each tribe, hence, promoting justice, equality, and efficiency.
pg054_p019: Planning is an integral part of the census; it is a key aspect in human development.
pg054_p020: Planning is about working for tomorrow while living today. With this understanding in the book of Numbers, the Israelites were obliged to plan how the Promised Land and its limited resources were to be distributed when the people finally entered the land. In order to plan well or accordingly, one needs a thorough investigation to obtain a detailed data and a clear mapping plan that is capable of facilitating demographic movement and encampment of a large community manageable.
pg054_p026: Apart from demographic issues, the book of Numbers provides liturgical data management. This implies that records pertaining to the offerings and gifts offered by the Israelites were all kept in the books. Numbers chapter seven provides a detailed account of the offerings that each tribe offered for the dedication of the altar.

pg054_p032: Judah were properly recorded, starting with the first day when Nahshon the son of

Statistically speaking, the book of Numbers shows that each tribe’s offerings were recorded with

pg070_p005: Among the qualities of a good citizen is the sense of patriotism; that is, the love for one’s nation and readiness to sacrifice for its development. In this chapter, you will learn the impotance of patriotism, bravery, humility, and perseverance according to the book of Joshua. The competencies developed will enable you to uphold and appreciate fundamental virtues of patriotism, bravery, humility, and perseverance.
pg070_p010: Think: The nation without patriotic people!
pg070_p011: Patriotism according to the book of Joshua
pg070_p012: Patriotism is a broad term that refers to: special affection for one’s nation; a sense of personal identification with the nation; special concern for the well-being of the nation; and, willingness to sacrifice to promote the nation’s good. Rightly put, patriotism is loyalty and a feeling of pride toward one’s nation or country. There is little difference between love and affection for one’s nation, and these terms are often used interchangeably. Furthermore, patriotism may involve feelings of love and devotion in national achievement, support for national values and willingness to contribute to the one’s nation development. However, the state of patriotism should not be used to promote ethnicity, culture, religious radicalism, or social division, instead it must be used as a call for true statesmanship and loyalty to the nation’s good.
pg070_p023: In the book of Joshua, patriotism is seen in relation to national identity and loyalty to God’s covenant. Joshua was loyal to God’s covenant and led the people according to God’s guidance (Joshua 23). Joshua also demonstrated his patriotism when he faithfully and obediently united his people, and led them to conquer and settle in the
pg070_p027: Promised Land (Joshua 5). Furthermore, patriotism in the book of Joshua is seen in Joshua’s ability to unite the twelve tribes of Israel in his leadership, and be able to share one faith (monotheism) and form a single national identity with common
pg071_im004: Page number 61 in a circular marker on a green footer band.
pg071_p004: destiny (Joshua 23). Good military leadership and techniques used in conquering the
pg071_p005: Promised Land are also considered as a sense of patriotism, as they were essential for victory in the establishment of their nation (Joshua 5:13-15).
pg071_p007: Unlike corrupt leaders and land-grabbers of our time, Joshua demonstrated his strong sense of patriotism through his equitable land acquisition and division to the twelve tribes of Israel, and he never used his power to assign any part of the land for himself (Joshua 12-21). Furthermore, patriotism is seen in Joshua’s act to insist that the sons of Israel remain faithful to God and avoid associating with the natives of the conquered land (Joshua 23:17). In his farewell, Joshua taught and reminded
pg071_p013: Israel on the importance of remaining faithful to God’s covenant. He reminded them to keep the covenant and remain faithful to God’s laws (Joshua 23:24).
pg071_p016: Importance of patriotism lies in its ability to foster a sense of belongingness and unity among citizens. It helps to conserve and celebrate a nation’s cultural heritage, including traditions and customs, and promoting social responsibility and accountability. Patriotism encourages individuals to contribute to their country’s progress through civic duties and volunteering. Furthermore, patriotism promotes public sacrifice which is essential for the functioning of a state and can reduce conflicts. Patriotism fosters national identity, helping individuals feel connected to their country and values. It enhances social cohesion and encourages collective efforts towards common goals. It is often found in a deep sense of patriotism, where people show enduring loyalty to their country and their fellow citizens. This love for one’s country goes beyond just celebrating national holidays. It is rather seen in how people treat each other and work for the community every day; it fosters national unity. When patriotic feelings are genuine and inclusive, they can transcend individual interests and foster a collective identity. This sense of unity is essential for a nation’s stability and growth, as united citizens are more likely to work together towards common goals and support one another in times of need.
pg071_p032: The roots of national unity through patriotism can be found in various elements such as shared celebrations, national holidays and historical milestones, where citizens come together irrespective of their backgrounds. Collective memories and stories of a nation’s past which imbue a common sense of heritage and destiny. National symbols like the flag, anthem, and emblems evoke feelings of connection to one’s homeland. However, for patriotism to truly unite people, it must be inclusive and respect the nation’s diversity. It should not only celebrate common histories and shared symbols, but also honour various cultures, languages, and traditions that contributed to the nation’s identity and development.

pg072_p007: Strength and bravery in the book of Joshua
pg072_p008: The commission of Joshua to lead the Israelites marked the transition of leadership from Moses to Joshua. This transition is significant not just for its historical context but also for its enduring lessons on faith, responsibility, and divine assurance (Joshua
pg072_p012: Strength and bravery are clear in the book of Joshua as demonstrated in life and mission of Joshua, offering insights into overcoming challenges through steadfast belief and obedience to God. God’s directives to Joshua to embody strength and bravery are not merely an encouragement but also a command that abridges the essence of his mission. This instruction is repeated several times, underscoring its importance. The repetition serves not just as a reminder but as a reinforcement of the mental and emotional fortitude required to lead a nation on the edge of enormous change.
pg072_p020: The word ‘strength’ as used in the Bible, has nothing to do with our physical strength but rather a spiritual strength which is given by God to us when we are weak and delicate. The spiritual strength is manifested in believers as they stand strong against the forces of deconstruction. Therefore, strength is a gift of the Lord that gives us an internal fortitude that enables us to stand firm for the sake of God and defending
pg072_p025: His truth. As Prophet Isaiah declared, “The Lord God is my strength and my song”
pg072_p026: (Isiah 12:2). Apostle Peter reminds us, “After you have suffered a little while, the
pg072_p027: God of all grace, who has called you to his eternal glory in Christ, will himself restore, confirm, strengthen, and establish you” (1 Peter 5:10). Bravery comprises of discipline, awareness, and insight. It calls for the ability to understand your strengths, having insights into what you want, and skillfully maneuvering your world to bring out the best to yourself and to those around you. Indeed, bravery is the state of having or showing mental or moral strength to face danger, fear or difficulty.
pg072_p033: Bravery can be physical like rescuing someone from danger, or moral, like standing up for your idea in the face of opposition. In a biblical sense, bravery isn’t just about maneuvering your world, but trusting in God’s power and promises, even when facing impossible challenges, as demonstrated by the biblical figures like Moses,
pg072_p037: Joshua, and Jesus. The Bible emphasises that true bravery stems from recognizing
pg072_p038: God’s presence and sustaining strengths, rather than relying on one’s own abilities.
pg073_im004: Page number 63 in a circular marker on a green decorative footer.
pg073_p004: Bravery involves facing fear and doubt, but not in a reckless or arrogant way, but rather with faith and reliance on God. Biblical examples of bravery often involve obeying God’s commands and remaining faithful, even when it is difficult. God told
pg073_p007: Joshua to “Be strong and courageous” as he led the Israelites into the Promised Land, emphasizing God’s presence and support. There are many indicators of bravery and strength in the book of Joshua:
pg073_p010: (1) God’s command to Joshua to be courageous and brave. Joshua accepted and practiced this in his mission. This is a typical indicator of strength and bravery.
pg073_p012: Joshua was supposed to rely on these virtues. In this context, strength extends beyond the battlefield. It demands bravery to make difficult decisions, to stand firm in one’s convictions, and to trust in a divinely ordained path yet without being worried with uncertainty (Joshua 1:6-9). (2) Another indicator of strength and bravery in the book of Joshua is the fact that Joshua accepted and fulfilled a difficult mission. Leading the people of Israel was not an easy task. The book of Joshua, therefore illustrates that true strength and bravery often involves stepping into roles or situations that challenge our comfort zones, and push us toward growth. This kind of strength and bravery is rooted in faith, serving as a reminder that belief in a higher purpose can empower individuals to evidently overcome the unconquerable obstacles (Joshua
pg073_p022: 1:9). (3) The book of Joshua indicates that strength and bravery are necessary in making difficult decision. This means that, to stand firm in one’s convictions, and to trust in the divinely ordained path without being worried about uncertainties as demonstrated by Joshua is not easy. Joshua followed God’s instructions and invited the people of Israel to stand steadfast in their faith to the true God (Joshua 23-24). (4)
pg073_p027: Furthermore, the book of Joshua indicates strength and bravery by showing Joshua heroically leading the Israelites to take over Canaan. With God’s providence Joshua surmounts the kings of Canaan. (5) Another indicator of strength and bravery in the book of Joshua is seen when Joshua took decision, and supervised the division of the land of Canaan among Jewish with such precision (Joshua 13-22). (6) Joshua in his farewell, admonished the people of Israel to stand firm in their faith to God, in case they go astray, on his part and his family will stand for God (Joshua 23-24).
pg073_p034: Bravery, humility and perseverance in the book of Joshua
pg073_p035: Bravery, humility and perseverance are virtues. A virtue implies a permanent disposition to perform good deeds. The following are some explanations on the importance of bravery, humility and perseverance.
pg074_p005: Bravery is a mental or moral strength to face danger and difficult situation with confidence and determination. It requires endurance because it requires persistence and perseverance. Sometimes bravery means being the person who stands out in the crowd, who speaks up, and who must be a voice, either the voice they need to hear, or a voice for others (Joshua 24:15). Occasionally, bravery means having prudence to pause, to sit in silence, and to be resilient. Furthermore, it means putting up the fight of your life, and fighting till the very end. Besides, it means raising up that white flag, accepting defeat, and find the will to move on from that defeat without anger, and with wisdom (Joshua 7:3).
pg074_p014: Sometimes bravery means to be grateful, contented, and satisfied with the state of your present conditions. But bravery which is an act of courage must also be an act of love and compassion. To be brave, you must accept that the great love of anything may result in heartbreak, and pain and disappointment. To be brave, you must be willing to risk the possibility of a terrifying ending. To be brave is to be alive and to live in such a way that the world knows you are afraid but you love more than you fear.

pg075_p008: Bravery is important for each individual’s life because it helps the person to trust in God and stand firm in faith, and it aids the person to work hard and take risk for personal development, and it enables the person to endure in difficult situation and danger. (4) Furthermore, bravery supports the person to accept rejection and failures as a lesson and not a defeat. (5) Additionally, bravery helps the person to trust on oneself and defend one’s own ideas, life and the life of others. (6) Besides, bravery makes the person avoid dangers of life and live a moral life. It helps one to take risk to achieve a high good (Josh 1:1-9).

pg075_p028: Humility is a quality of having a modest view of one’s importance. In the Bible, humility is described as meekness, lowliness, and absence of self. Humility is an internal attitude of the person, not merely an outward manifestation of one’s behaviour.
pg075_p031: It is indeed an attitude of spiritual modesty that comes from understanding our place in the larger order of things. It does not entail taking our desires, successes, or failing too seriously (Joshua 1:7-9;13; 19:49-51). The word humility appears several times throughout the Bible. Wherever we read about humility in the Bible, we see that this trait is something God desires for His people. Humility is beneficial for us, for God, and for those around us. St. Paul teaches us that “do nothing out of selfish ambition or vain conceit, rather in humility value others above yourself” (Philippians 2:3).

pg076_p004: Humility is a virtue which involves a balanced self-awareness, recognizing one’s place in life while maintaining strength and courage, and prioritizing social harmony over self-importance. Humility is important to make one cooperate with others, and it fosters learning and growth. It encourages willingness to learn for the benefit of others. Humility strengthens relationships and promotes personal growth by allowing individuals to acknowledge their strengths and weaknesses, thus accepting feedback from others, and exposing them to new ideas. Again, humility builds trust and stronger relationships. Humble people are more approachable, emphatic and likely to consider others’ viewpoints. Furthermore, humility promotes self-awareness, enhance leadership engagement, reduce arrogance, cultivate empathy and compassion, and promote positive outlook etc. Humility creates willingness to work for and serve others (Joshua 24:13).

pg077_p005: Perseverance is defined as persistence in doing something despite difficulty or delay in achieving the intended goals and purposes. It is often an underestimated virtue that is critical for anyone trying to get ahead in life. Life as we know is never a straight line. It is filled with a lot of twists and turns. For one to be successful, whether, in business or in social life, one must learn the art of perseverance, that is walking with others instead of walking alone at the expense of others. Perseverance is what will keep you going when everything else seems to be working slowly or against you. More often, perseverance is a virtue that separates the winners from the losers. Remember, winning does not mean that the winner encountered lesser challenges or difficulties than the loser. It means that the winner persevered through countless storms of difficulties.
pg077_p017: Perseverance is an incredibly valuable trait that can help us attain our goals and be successful in life. It allows us to keep going even when we face obstacles or difficulties, giving us the strength to keep pushing forward until we get the desired results. Perseverance makes one able to quickly bounce back from setbacks with less difficulty. Perseverance can help you to stay motivated and focused on your
pg077_p022: goals, meaning that you are more likely to be successful in achieving them. With perseverance, you will be more likely to take risks and try new things, as well as being patient focusing at something until it pays. It also leads to achieve difficult goals. Being able to persevere means you can work hard and stay motivated even
pg077_p026: when you feel like making little progress toward achieving your goals. In life, it is normally easy to give up when things are tough, but if you have the strength and resilience of perseverance, you will more likely be able to achieve the goals you set for yourself.
